name: Salmon calcitonin
lead: Salmon calcitonin is a synthetic version of calcitonin, a 32-amino-acid peptide hormone made by thyroid C cells that lowers blood calcium by inhibiting bone resorption. The salmon form differs from the human sequence at 16 residues and is more potent and longer acting.[1][2][3]

It is a prescription bone-resorption inhibitor. Its US injection label lists symptomatic Paget's disease of bone, hypercalcaemia and, when alternatives are unsuitable, postmenopausal osteoporosis; nasal-spray formulations have also been marketed.[2][3] Its connection to appearance is through the skeleton: by slowing bone breakdown it is used to preserve bone in conditions that can change bone shape or lose bone mass, which is the framing most relevant to someone interested in skeletal structure.[2] No looksmaxxing-community discussion or appearance-related study of salmon calcitonin has been found.

Research on salmon calcitonin spans bone microstructure in postmenopausal women, fracture-related pain and muscle strength, and osteoarthritis, with several trials registered in the United States.[4][5][6]

paras: Wikipedia lists postmenopausal osteoporosis, hypercalcaemia, bone metastases, Paget's disease of bone and phantom limb pain among the uses of salmon calcitonin, and notes investigation for spinal stenosis.[3] The US label limits the injection to Paget's disease, hypercalcaemia and osteoporosis when alternatives are unsuitable, and says the need for continued therapy should be re-evaluated periodically because of a possible association with malignancy.[2]
No cosmetic or looksmaxxing use is documented.

Paget's disease of bone is the clearest example of a condition where calcitonin intersects with visible bone shape. Wikipedia describes abnormal bone remodeling, excessive breakdown followed by disorganized new formation, that can lead to deformity, pain and fractures; skull involvement can cause frontal bossing and an increased hat size, and bowing of an affected femur can distort leg alignment [15]. It is mostly a disease of older adults, rare under age 55, affecting about 1.5 to 8 percent of the population overall and more men than women [15].

Within that picture, bisphosphonates are the most commonly prescribed treatment, while synthetic salmon calcitonin is given by injection for 6 to 18 months, is seldom used, and has a debated safety profile [15]. This is the setting in which the peptide is relevant to skeletal structure, and it is a medical rather than cosmetic use.

The label describes calcitonin salmon as a calcitonin receptor agonist acting mainly on bone, with direct renal and gastrointestinal effects also recognised; calcitonin receptors are found on osteoclasts and osteoblasts, though the hormone's role in normal human bone physiology is described as not fully elucidated [2]. Grokipedia states it inhibits osteoclast function via G protein-coupled signalling [1].

The hormone binds a G protein-coupled receptor found mainly on osteoclasts and also in kidney and brain cells, raising intracellular cAMP; the kidney effect on calcium and phosphate is described as minor in humans, and kidneys become resistant with sustained exposure.[3] The calcitonin receptor can also pair with receptor-activity-modifying proteins to form amylin receptors, and salmon calcitonin binds the core receptor on its own; a 2022 preclinical paper reports antidepressant-like effects through amylin receptors.[7][8][9]

Salmon calcitonin was historically extracted from fish glands. The version used today is made by recombinant DNA or chemical synthesis.[3] The calcitonin gene is also alternatively spliced to produce calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), a separate neuropeptide studied in migraine and vascular biology.[3][10]

Douglas Copp and B. Cheney first purified calcitonin in 1962 at the University of British Columbia; Copp named it for its role in keeping calcium levels normal. It was initially thought to come from the parathyroid gland until Iain Macintyre's team in London showed that thyroid parafollicular cells secrete it [3]. Early sources were fish glands, and salmon calcitonin proved more active than the human hormone; today it is produced by recombinant DNA or chemical synthesis, and these forms are described as pharmacologically equivalent [3].
A trade report states calcitonin salmon has been marketed in the United States since 1975 [16].

The label lists hypersensitivity reactions including reports of fatal anaphylaxis, hypocalcaemia, and malignancy, noting a meta-analysis of 21 clinical trials suggesting an increased risk of overall malignancies in calcitonin-treated patients; common adverse reactions are nausea with or without vomiting, injection-site inflammation and facial or hand flushing, and circulating antibodies may reduce response [2].

In July 2012 the European Medicines Agency's CHMP concluded that calcitonin's limited efficacy for preventing vertebral fractures in postmenopausal osteoporosis did not outweigh its risks, recommended withdrawal of the nasal spray (used only for osteoporosis) and proposed restricting injectable use to short-term indications such as acute bone loss from immobilization, Paget's disease when alternatives cannot be used, and cancer-related hypercalcaemia [16].

In March 2013 a joint FDA advisory committee meeting voted 12 to 9 that the benefit-risk data did not support salmon calcitonin nasal spray for osteoporosis, and 20 to 1 that future products seeking that indication should supply fracture-efficacy data. Pooled manufacturer analyses showed an odds ratio of 1.6 for malignancy against placebo, with basal cell carcinoma most common, though FDA presenters noted that the result was heavily influenced by one large five-year trial [16]. Wikipedia's Paget's article states that a meta-analysis found a causal link to cancer unlikely while not ruling out a weak association, and that EMA restricted calcitonin use in Paget's disease to about three months [15]. The current US label retains the statement about a possible malignancy association [2].

Besides bone conditions, Wikipedia lists phantom limb pain among reported uses and mentions a small study of subcutaneous calcitonin in women with type 2 diabetes and osteoporosis that reported fewer fractures, plus short-term benefit in mania with no further work reported [3].

A phase 3 trial of nasal salmon calcitonin enrolled 90 postmenopausal women to examine bone microstructure.[4] A phase 4 trial of 300 postmenopausal women examined nasal salmon calcitonin for muscle strength and pain after forearm fracture.[5] A phase 3 trial of oral salmon calcitonin in 1,030 patients with knee osteoarthritis was terminated.[6]

Randomised work in other settings includes a 60-patient trial in recent kidney-transplant recipients comparing alfacalcidol, alendronate, intranasal salmon calcitonin and control for post-transplant bone loss, and newer registered trials in pelvic ring injuries, herpes zoster pain and spinal-cord-injury neuropathic pain.[11][12][13][14] The label states that fracture-reduction efficacy for osteoporosis has not been demonstrated.[2] No studies of salmon calcitonin for height, facial structure or other appearance goals were found.

timeline.event: Douglas Copp and B. Cheney purify calcitonin at the University of British Columbia; Iain Macintyre's team later traces it to the thyroid C cells.[3]
Calcitonin salmon is first marketed in the United States [16].
Alternative RNA processing of the calcitonin gene is reported, leading to the discovery of CGRP.[10]
A randomised trial compares intranasal salmon calcitonin with other agents for post-transplant bone loss.[11]
EMA's CHMP recommends withdrawing nasal calcitonin and limiting injectable use [16].
FDA advisory committees vote 12-9 that benefit-risk data do not support the nasal spray for osteoporosis [16].

card.summary: A fish-derived calcitonin used for Paget's disease and hypercalcaemia; it slows bone loss and has no documented appearance use.
card.note: Label warns of anaphylaxis, hypocalcaemia and a possible malignancy signal.

quick.overview:
Salmon calcitonin is a prescription peptide that slows bone breakdown. Doctors use it for Paget's disease of bone, high blood calcium and, when other drugs are unsuitable, postmenopausal osteoporosis.

No source reviewed shows looksmaxxing use or tests it for appearance.
quick.mechanism: It activates calcitonin receptors on bone-resorbing osteoclasts, reducing bone breakdown and calcium release.
quick.risks: The label lists anaphylaxis, low calcium, nausea, flushing and a possible increased malignancy risk. It is Rx-only.

angle.text: Salmon calcitonin is a clinical bone drug, so any link to looks runs through preserving bone in conditions such as Paget's disease or postmenopausal bone loss rather than reshaping a healthy face or frame. It has no documented cosmetic use.[2]
